items.title: How do I know which assessment I need?
items.desc: Our team can help you choose the most appropriate assessment based on your needs and goals. During your free consultation, we'll ask a few questions about what you're looking for and guide you towards the right option.

items.title: What happens during a free consultation?
items.desc: A friendly member of our team listens to your concerns, explains how our assessments work and answers your questions. There is no obligation and no pressure to book anything afterwards.

items.title: Are Fairneuro assessments completed online?
items.desc: Most assessments are completed online using secure video consultation, which suits the majority of people. In-person appointments are available where they are clinically appropriate.

items.title: What does the online screener do?
items.desc: Our online screeners are quick, research-based questionnaires designed to identify patterns and highlight whether a full assessment may be helpful. They are not diagnostic, but a valuable starting point.

items.title: Will I receive a report after my assessment?
items.desc: Yes. You receive a detailed written report explaining the findings, whether diagnostic criteria are met, your strengths and challenges, and personalised recommendations for what comes next.

items.title: What happens if I receive a diagnosis?
items.desc: We talk you through what the diagnosis means in practical terms, and help you decide which recommendations to act on first. A diagnosis is the beginning of support, not the end of the process.

items.title: Do you offer support after diagnosis?
items.desc: We do. Coaching, education, workplace and wellbeing support are all available, and our post-diagnostic support helps you turn understanding into practical everyday strategies.

items.title: Can parents enquire about assessments for children?
items.desc: Absolutely. Parents and carers are welcome to get in touch at any point. We will explain the process, what your child can expect, and how we involve families throughout.

items.title: Who is this quiz for?
items.desc: Adults who recognise something of themselves in descriptions of ADHD and want a structured way to check whether it is worth exploring. It asks about the past six months of adult life, so it is not designed for children — if you are a parent wondering about your child, our child ADHD assessment page is the better starting point.

items.title: How accurate is it?
items.desc: It uses the ASRS-v1.1, the screening checklist developed with the World Health Organization and used widely in adult ADHD services. Six of the eighteen questions form the screener itself: four or more qualifying answers there indicates symptoms highly consistent with adult ADHD and means a full assessment is worth considering. It is a good filter, not a verdict — it will flag some people who turn out not to have ADHD, and miss some who do.

items.title: How is it scored?
items.desc: Each question has a threshold — for some, answering "Sometimes" already counts; for others it takes "Often". Answers at or above that threshold are counted as qualifying answers. Separately, every answer scores from 0 for "Never" to 4 for "Very Often", giving an intensity score that reflects how strongly you experience these traits rather than simply whether you do.

items.title: What are the main symptoms of ADHD in adults?
items.desc: Inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity are the two recognised clusters, but adults often notice the knock-on effects more: difficulty starting or finishing tasks, losing track of time, forgetfulness, disorganisation, restlessness, interrupting, emotional intensity and rapid mood shifts, difficulty switching off, and patterns of leaving jobs, courses or projects unfinished.

items.title: Can ADHD be self-diagnosed?
items.desc: No. NICE guidance (NG87) is clear that a diagnosis of ADHD can only be made by a specialist psychiatrist, paediatrician or other appropriately qualified healthcare professional with training and expertise in diagnosing ADHD, following a full clinical and psychosocial assessment. A quiz can tell you whether that assessment is worth booking — nothing more.

items.title: How is ADHD actually diagnosed?
items.desc: Through a full diagnostic assessment with a qualified clinician: a detailed history of your life from childhood onwards, a structured diagnostic interview such as the DIVA-5, information from someone who knows you well where that is possible, and consideration of other explanations and co-occurring conditions. Symptoms are then mapped against the DSM-5 criteria.

items.title: What happens if I score highly?
items.desc: Nothing automatically — the result is yours and stays in your browser. If you would like to talk it through, you can book a free, no-obligation consultation with our team, and we will help you decide whether a full ADHD assessment makes sense for you.
